title: Why Post-Quantum Cryptography Matters for TLS 1.3
summary: TLS 1.3 can combine classical elliptic-curve exchange with ML-KEM. Understand the new IETF hybrid groups, security rationale, and deployment tradeoffs.
body: TLS protects an enormous amount of Internet traffic, but the security of a TLS connection depends on several different cryptographic operations. The key-establishment stage is especially important to the post-quantum transition: if an attacker records encrypted traffic today, a sufficiently capable future quantum computer could threaten confidentiality when the session's secret depended only on quantum-vulnerable public-key mathematics. Standards bodies are addressing that exposure by defining hybrid key exchange for TLS 1.3.
What changes in a TLS handshake?

In a conventional TLS 1.3 handshake, client and server negotiate cryptographic parameters and derive shared secrets used to protect the connection. Elliptic-curve Diffie–Hellman exchange is widely used for this purpose. Its security relies on mathematical problems that a large, fault-tolerant quantum computer could attack with quantum algorithms. The post-quantum question is therefore not whether TLS uses encryption at all, but how the two parties agree on the secrets that feed that encryption.

NIST's FIPS 203 defines ML-KEM, a key encapsulation mechanism based on the module learning-with-errors problem. A KEM allows parties to establish a shared secret over a public channel. The resulting secret can then support symmetric encryption and authentication. ML-KEM is not itself a replacement for every part of TLS: it does not replace the record-layer encryption algorithm, certificate validation or the entire protocol.

The IETF's RFC 9954, published in July 2026, describes how multiple key-exchange algorithms can be combined within TLS 1.3. The objective is that the resulting exchange can remain secure if all but one of its components resist attack. In the current transition, the practical combination is a traditional elliptic-curve exchange plus a post-quantum KEM.
The standardized hybrid groups
RFC 10024, published in August 2026 as an Internet Standards Track document, specifies three post-quantum/traditional hybrid key-agreement mechanisms for TLS 1.3:

Named groupTraditional componentPost-quantum component
X25519MLKEM768X25519ML-KEM-768
SecP256r1MLKEM768secp256r1ML-KEM-768
SecP384r1MLKEM1024secp384r1ML-KEM-1024

These are named groups, not three interchangeable spellings for one algorithm. A client and server need compatible support to negotiate a particular group. The ML-KEM suffix indicates the NIST parameter set; the traditional component indicates the elliptic-curve method paired with it. RFC 10024 supplies the protocol definition rather than leaving each vendor to invent its own combination.

The design is called hybrid because both components contribute to key establishment. It does not mean that a TLS connection automatically runs two complete independent TLS handshakes. Nor does the term mean that the post-quantum component has been proved unbreakable. The value of combining different assumptions is that an unforeseen weakness in one component need not immediately expose the shared secret if the other component remains secure under the construction's assumptions.
What hybrid TLS does not solve

A TLS deployment still needs server authentication. Certificates and their signatures are a distinct migration problem from the ephemeral key exchange. Replacing the latter with an ML-KEM hybrid does not by itself turn an RSA- or ECDSA-signed certificate chain into a post-quantum signature chain. NIST standardized ML-DSA under FIPS 204 and SLH-DSA under FIPS 205 for digital signatures, while FIPS 203 addresses key encapsulation. These roles should not be conflated in architecture diagrams or compliance reports.

Likewise, adding ML-KEM does not repair certificate misissuance, weak endpoint security, compromised application secrets or incorrect trust-store configuration. Hybrid key exchange addresses a specific cryptographic risk: the establishment of session keys against classical and future quantum threats. Existing TLS operational controls still matter.
Deployment questions for operators

Suppose an organization runs TLS at a cloud load balancer, an API gateway and an application server. Updating the application library alone may accomplish nothing for public-facing traffic if the load balancer actually terminates the external TLS session. The team should first identify each termination point, record the negotiated groups in testing and check whether clients, proxies and monitoring systems handle the new handshake material correctly.

A realistic pilot should measure connection establishment under normal and constrained network conditions. ML-KEM uses different public-key and ciphertext sizes from classical elliptic-curve exchanges, so implementers should examine handshake bytes, fragmentation, retransmissions and compatibility with middleboxes. The relevant comparison is an end-to-end connection through the actual network path, not a standalone algorithm benchmark.

Operators should also decide what happens when a peer does not support a hybrid group. A deployment can only claim post-quantum protection for connections that actually negotiate an appropriate mechanism. A server configuration flag, by itself, does not establish that every client session received the new protection. Negotiation telemetry and clearly defined fallback policy are essential to making deployment claims accurate.
Why the timing matters

NIST finalized FIPS 203 in August 2024, while the IETF published the TLS hybrid design and named-group standards in 2026. Those milestones make interoperable implementation more concrete, but do not mean that every TLS stack has deployed the new groups. The urgency stems partly from the possibility that encrypted data captured today could remain valuable to an adversary in the future. Organizations should therefore prioritize long-lived sensitive data, test interoperable implementations and distinguish hybrid key establishment from the separate work of migrating digital signatures.

title: What Is Shor's Algorithm, and Why Does It Threaten RSA?
summary: Shor’s algorithm uses quantum period finding to factor integers efficiently. See a small worked example, the RSA connection, and the hardware limitations.
body: Shor's algorithm is the reason quantum computing appears in discussions of Internet security. Introduced by mathematician Peter Shor in 1994, it gives a quantum computer an efficient route to factoring large integers and solving related discrete-logarithm problems. Those are precisely the kinds of problems that underpin widely deployed public-key systems. The important qualification is that the algorithm's mathematical efficiency does not mean today's quantum hardware can routinely break real-world RSA keys.
Why factoring matters

Multiplying two large prime numbers is straightforward for an ordinary computer. Reversing the process (finding the prime factors when only their product is known) becomes difficult for appropriately chosen large inputs. RSA relies on this asymmetry. The public modulus is a product of two secret primes; knowledge of the factors makes it possible to derive information needed to recover the private key from the public parameters.

For a toy example, take 15 = 3 × 5. A human can factor 15 immediately, so there is no security significance in this particular number. The point is to show the structure of the computation. Real cryptographic moduli are vastly larger, and their factors are not obvious. Classical factoring algorithms improve on naive trial division, but no known general-purpose classical polynomial-time factoring algorithm makes appropriately sized RSA moduli easy to break.

NIST explains that Shor's 1994 work transformed quantum computing into a national-security concern because a sufficiently capable machine could factor numbers that conventional cryptographic systems rely on keeping difficult to factor. The concern is specifically about public-key mathematical assumptions, not a claim that all encryption becomes instantly useless.
From factoring to period finding

The key insight is to turn factoring into a problem of finding a period, also called an order. Choose an integer a that is relatively prime to the number N to be factored. Examine the sequence of powers of a modulo N. Because there are only finitely many possible residues, the sequence repeats. Its period r is the smallest positive integer satisfying a^r ≡ 1 (mod N).
Take N = 15 and a = 2. The successive residues are:

PowerResidue modulo 15
2¹2
2²4
2³8
2⁴1

The period is therefore r = 4. Because r is even, compute 2^(r/2) = 4. Then calculate gcd(4 − 1, 15) = 3 and gcd(4 + 1, 15) = 5. These greatest common divisors reveal the two nontrivial factors of 15.

This example shows why period finding is useful: the period can provide a route to factors through ordinary arithmetic. It also shows why not every choice works. If the selected number shares a factor with N, the greatest-common-divisor step may already expose one; if the period is odd or produces an unhelpful value, the procedure may need another choice. Shor's algorithm is probabilistic rather than a magic single-operation factorizer.
Where the quantum speedup enters

A classical computer can perform the modular arithmetic and greatest-common-divisor calculations. The hard part for large numbers is obtaining the useful period efficiently. Shor's quantum subroutine prepares a superposition, applies modular exponentiation and uses quantum Fourier-transform techniques to extract information about periodicity from measurement outcomes. Classical post-processing then reconstructs a candidate period and tests whether it yields factors.

The quantum Fourier transform is not a device that reads every value of a superposition into a classical list. Measurement yields limited classical information, and the algorithm is designed so interference makes that information useful. Multiple runs and checks can be needed. This distinction matters because popular descriptions sometimes imply that a quantum computer simply tries all candidate factors in parallel and reads the answer. That is not how the algorithm works.

Shor's algorithm is often described as offering an exponential improvement over the best known classical approaches to the relevant mathematical problems. This is a statement about asymptotic computational complexity. It does not remove the substantial costs of reliable quantum gates, error correction, physical qubits, classical control or the implementation of modular arithmetic at cryptographic sizes.
Which cryptography is affected?

RSA is the clearest example because factoring its public modulus undermines its central assumption. Quantum algorithms for discrete logarithms also threaten traditional Diffie–Hellman and elliptic-curve public-key mechanisms. That means the exposure spans both key establishment and digital signatures, though these are different functions and require different replacements.

NIST finalized FIPS 203 (ML-KEM) for post-quantum key encapsulation, FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) for digital signatures and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA) for stateless hash-based signatures in August 2024. The standards address the need to move away from vulnerable public-key schemes before a future large-scale quantum computer becomes practical. They do not imply that a cryptographically relevant quantum computer already exists.
What Shor's algorithm does not prove

The algorithm does not demonstrate that any announced processor with a particular raw qubit count can factor production RSA keys. Raw physical-qubit counts omit crucial information about error rates, circuit depth, connectivity and the overhead of fault tolerance. A useful security assessment therefore separates three questions: whether the mathematics gives a quantum advantage, whether a hardware platform can execute the required computation reliably, and when a specific cryptographic deployment must migrate.

It also does not establish that every cryptographic primitive is equally vulnerable. Symmetric-key encryption and cryptographic hashes face different quantum attack models from RSA factoring. The practical response is to inventory public-key dependencies, use standardized post-quantum replacements where appropriate and avoid treating speculative hardware dates as security guarantees.

title: Diraq switches on an eight qubit silicon spin quantum computer inside Equinix Sydney
summary: Diraq says its silicon spin system is live in a commercial data centre, draws under 20 kW and is targeted to reach 256 qubits within a year.
body: Sydney based Diraq says its silicon spin quantum computer is now live inside an Equinix data centre in Sydney, which it describes as the first deployment of a silicon spin system in a commercial data centre. The company made the announcement this week.
What is running
The system currently operates with eight qubits. Diraq says it is targeting up to 256 qubits in the same deployed machine within the next year, which is a goal rather than a demonstrated capability.

Diraq builds its qubits in silicon using the same CMOS manufacturing processes used for conventional chips. The company argues that this lets customers add computing power by upgrading the quantum processor, with minimal changes to the surrounding infrastructure.
Power and space

The current machine draws less than 20 kW and occupies about 16 square metres, according to Business News Australia. Diraq expects a future utility scale system to draw around 300 kW, which it says is less than a third of a single next generation AI rack, and to need as little as about 5 square metres.

The facility hosts computing for customers in banking, healthcare, utilities, manufacturing and retail. When the deployment was first announced in September, the companies said the system's cryogenic cooling and control electronics were self contained, and that testing in the live environment would come before partners and customers were invited to see it in action.
Equinix's view

Equinix executive vice president Harmeen Mehta called the deployment "an important proof point for quantum," saying it shows a path for these systems to run alongside existing enterprise infrastructure.
What it does and does not show

Putting a quantum computer inside a working data centre tests practical questions such as power, cooling, footprint and integration with conventional systems. It does not by itself show that an eight qubit machine can outperform classical computers on useful problems. The more telling milestone will be whether Diraq reaches its 256 qubit target in the same system, and what error rates it reports along the way.
Diraq is one of several companies betting that qubits made with standard semiconductor processes will scale more easily than other approaches.

title: Quantum Computing Inc posts $9.5 million quarterly revenue as acquisitions kick in
summary: QCi's third quarter revenue beat its whole first half total, driven by acquired photonics and packaging businesses. It lost $15.1 million and holds about $1.3 billion.
body: Quantum Computing Inc, the Hoboken, New Jersey company known as QCi, reported third quarter revenue of $9.5 million on Monday, more than the $9.2 million it booked in the whole first half of 2026. The results release shows that most of the growth came from businesses it bought this year rather than from quantum computers.
Where the revenue came from

QCi said growth was driven mainly by three companies acquired in the first half: Luminar Semiconductors, NuCrypt and NHanced Semiconductors. They sell photonic components, quantum communications products and advanced packaging services to aerospace, government and industrial customers. Revenue a year earlier was just $384 thousand.
Margins and losses

Gross profit was about $428 thousand, a gross margin of 4.5%. Operating expenses rose to $29.0 million from $10.5 million, which the company put down to higher personnel costs, expanded research and development, sales and marketing, and about $1.0 million of acquisition costs.
Interest and other income of $13.0 million helped offset that. The net loss was $15.1 million, or $0.07 per basic share.
A large cash cushion

QCi ended September with about $1.3 billion in cash, cash equivalents and investments, including $174.3 million in cash and $1.1 billion in short and long term investments. Contract backlog was about $39.1 million.
Quantum work

On the quantum side, the company highlighted a framework agreement with Hamad Bin Khalifa University in Qatar that includes cloud access to its Dirac 3 optimisation system, and a commercial agreement with INmune Bio to apply its Dirac technology alongside AI to clinical data. QCi called the INmune Bio deal its first commercial customer in pharmaceuticals and biotechnology.
Reading the numbers

The jump in revenue is real, but it reflects established photonics and packaging businesses rather than sales of quantum processors, and the 4.5% gross margin shows the combined company is still far from profitable operations. Chief executive Yuping Huang said the focus is "increasingly shifting from what we can build to what we can put to work for customers."

title: Abu Dhabi Maritime Academy partners with Quincus and Quantinuum on quantum research
summary: ADMA, Quincus and Quantinuum will study quantum, AI and high-performance computing for maritime operations, logistics and mining. No operational quantum advantage is claimed.
body: Abu Dhabi Maritime Academy (ADMA), part of AD Ports Group, has announced a research partnership with Quincus and Quantinuum to explore quantum computing, artificial intelligence and high-performance computing for maritime operations, transport logistics and mining, The Quantum Insider reported on November 9. The announcement was made at Quantum Innovation Summit 2026 in Dubai.
The report describes a research collaboration, not a finished commercial product or a measured quantum speedup.
What the partners say they will do

According to The Quantum Insider, the partners will start by identifying operational challenges and then assess where advanced computing could improve processes across the three sectors. That is a narrower commitment than announcing a working optimisation product. The report does not name a specific algorithm, dataset, quantum processor or performance target for the work.
Earlier maritime quantum work

The academy previously signed a memorandum of understanding with Vernewell Group and launched the Blue Initiative in October 2025. That earlier programme covers communications, sensing and optimisation alongside education and industry engagement. The new collaboration adds named technology partners. The Quantum Insider does not disclose a budget, project timetable or research milestones.
What is still missing

A meaningful assessment will need concrete use cases and comparisons with established classical methods. That distinction matters for optimisation, where classical software already handles many industrial problems. A later study might show quantum techniques helping in a defined setting; it would not automatically imply broad superiority.

For now, the November 9 announcement establishes the collaboration and its intended research areas. It does not establish that a quantum computer has improved shipping schedules, mining operations or transport costs.

title: IBM patent filing describes sharing quantum processors by reusing noise models
summary: IBM's "Quantum Queue Optimization for Error Mitigation" application describes a scheduler that groups compatible jobs on one chip and reuses stored noise models to cut repeated error-mitigation work.
body: IBM is seeking patent protection for a method that would let several users share one quantum processor while reducing the work needed for error mitigation, The Quantum Insider reported on November 9. The application is titled "Quantum Queue Optimization for Error Mitigation." The Quantum Insider says it was filed on May 5, 2025.
The filing describes a proposed system. It does not report measured gains in throughput, waiting times or cost.
The problem it targets

According to the report, the application addresses two sources of waste. First, a program may need only part of a processor's qubits, but exclusive access leaves the other qubits idle. Second, some error-mitigation methods need extra experiments to learn how noise affects particular groups of gates, and that work gets repeated.
Running jobs side by side can cause crosstalk, which changes the errors that have to be accounted for. IBM's approach builds those effects into the decision about which programs to run together.
How the scheduler would work

- Reuse noise models: the system would store noise models, which describe the errors tied to specific operations, and look for queued programs whose combined operations match a model it already has. - Match connectivity: a model applies only to the same set of active qubit connections. A model measured for one pattern does not automatically cover another, even a subset. - Keep models fresh: because noise drifts, the system would update frequently used models and drop stale ones. It could move a queued job forward so it runs while a matching model is still valid. - Fill gaps: if one job finishes on its qubits while another is still running, more work could be fitted into the opening without lengthening the run.
The filing gives an example on a 127-qubit processor. One program uses 52 qubits and another uses 30, with four unused qubits between them to limit crosstalk.
Policies, users and billing

The application describes three sharing policies. The strictest combines jobs only when the needed noise models already exist. A second allows new measurements and saves the resulting models. A third derives the needed noise information from existing models. The choice could depend on queue length, available resources, interference and job priority. Machine learning could help decide where programs run.

Users would control whether and how their jobs are shared, and the billing system could offer rebates to encourage participation. The filing lists interference, possible information leakage between users and coordination difficulty as challenges.

The inventors listed, according to Patentlyze as cited by The Quantum Insider, are Ana Paula Appel, Daniel Josef Egger, Kaelyn Jae Ferris, Sanjay Kumar Lalta Prasad Vishwakarma and Razvan Paul Sebastian Brandhofer. The Quantum Insider has previously covered Columbia Engineering's HyperQ, a quantum virtual machine approach to sharing processors that was tested on IBM hardware.

title: Oxford trapped-ion experiment shows Aharonov-Bohm interference in a lattice gauge theory loop
summary: Using two strontium ions, Oxford researchers simulated a Z2 lattice gauge theory loop in which zero flux doubled a particle's tunneling and a vison flux froze it, according to a Nature Physics study.
body: Researchers at the University of Oxford have used trapped ions to simulate the Aharonov-Bohm effect in a lattice gauge theory, according to a Nature Physics study described by Phys.org on November 7. The experiment built a quasi-two-dimensional loop so the team could see how magnetic flux affects a moving particle. Most earlier simulations of the simplest version of the theory could not show this.
Why loops matter

Lattice gauge theories model space as a grid, with matter at the sites and gauge fields on the links between them. In the simplest Z2 version, each link holds one of two values: a field line is either present or absent. Phys.org notes that Z2 theories are used to describe quantum spin liquids and high-temperature superconductors and are relevant to topological quantum error correction.

Most quantum simulations of Z2 theories have been one-dimensional, where links cannot form closed loops and flux effects cannot appear. Some two-dimensional experiments removed the matter fields, so they could not show how charges and fields affect each other.
Ions doing double duty

The Oxford team used a hybrid approach. Two electronic levels of a strontium ion served as a qubit representing the gauge field on a link, while the ion's vibrations stored matter. A single phonon represented one matter particle. Laser-driven forces made the phonon hop between sites, and each hop flipped the link's field line, tying the particle's motion to the gauge field.
"The advantage is that matter fields can be stored much more efficiently in the vibrational modes," said first author Sebastian Saner.
What they saw

With one ion and one link, the particle tunneled back and forth while the field line switched on and off, which is consistent with the Z2 version of Gauss's law. When the researchers added an energy cost for creating a field line, tunneling became faster but smaller. They describe this suppression as a precursor to confinement.
Adding a second ion created a second link, so the particle had two paths around a loop. Entangling the two link qubits encoded the flux:
- Zero flux: both paths added up, and the particle tunneled twice as fast as on a single link. - Nonzero flux (a "vison"): the paths canceled out, and the particle stayed where it started.
The flux stayed constant apart from slow decay due to decoherence. Numerical simulations that included known noise sources matched the data.
Next steps

Saner said the single loop "can easily be solved using classical computers," but that "even a relatively modest increase in lattice size could make the problem very difficult, if not impossible in practice" to simulate classically. The team also wants to extend the approach to Zn gauge theories with more field values.

title: UK FCA launches regulator-led quantum experimentation group to tackle financial crime
summary: The UK Financial Conduct Authority will launch a Quantum Experimentation Group in Q1 2027 to test whether quantum machine learning can help detect money laundering and fraud, using an FCA synthetic dataset. Registration closes 31 December 2026.
body: The UK Financial Conduct Authority will bring together financial firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories to test how quantum computing could help fight financial crime, it announced on 5 November. The FCA says its Quantum Experimentation Group, launching in the first quarter of 2027, will be the world's first regulator-led quantum computing experimentation group.
What the group will test

The group will first explore whether quantum machine learning can help detect money laundering and fraud. Participants will work on an FCA synthetic dataset, artificially generated data meant to get around one of the main barriers to testing: access to suitable data. The FCA will define the problem statements and work alongside participants.
Jessica Rusu, the FCA's chief data, information and intelligence officer, said early experimentation is "essential to understanding its potential in financial services."
Who can join

Financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories can register their interest by 31 December 2026. The FCA says the group will support organisations at every stage, from those just exploring use cases to those already running advanced experiments.
Why it matters

The initiative is an experiment, not a deployed supervisory tool, and the FCA does not claim quantum methods already beat conventional fraud detection. It says the group will help it understand the technology's opportunities and limits, the barriers to testing, and what they could mean for regulation.

summary: D-Wave said it won a 2026 Digital Innovation Award in the Quantum Computing and High-Performance Computing category for its project to deploy an Advantage2 annealing quantum computer in Italy with Swiss Quantum Technology and the Q-Alliance.
body: Short answer: D-Wave said on X on 6 November 2026 that it won a 2026 Digital Innovation Award in the Quantum Computing and High-Performance Computing category for a project titled "Italy's First Annealing Quantum Computer: D-Wave's Advantage2™ System."

According to the post, D-Wave is working with Swiss Quantum Technology SA and the Q-Alliance to deploy an Advantage2 annealing quantum computer in Italy. The company said the goal is to "expand access to quantum computing for businesses and researchers, support workforce training, and accelerate practical applications."
D-Wave added that Nicole Scourti, its Government Affairs Lead for EMEA, accepted the award in Italy last month, and thanked the Digital Innovation Forum organisers and its partners.
How to read it

This is an industry award for a deployment project, not a new hardware result or a performance benchmark. The post does not give an installation date, a customer list or contract value for the Italian system. Annealing machines such as Advantage2 are designed for optimisation problems and differ from the gate-based systems most rivals are building.
Photon Dispatch treats the 6 November post as the public record for the award and the Italy project description.

title: UK's National Quantum Computing Centre signs Phasecraft software licence for SparQ users
summary: The UK National Quantum Computing Centre has signed an enterprise licence with Phasecraft, giving UK businesses, researchers and public sector users access to its Magritte, Monet and Mondrian quantum software. Applications open in late November 2026.
body: The UK's National Quantum Computing Centre (NQCC) has signed an enterprise licence agreement with quantum algorithms company Phasecraft, giving UK organisations access to Phasecraft's software through the NQCC's SparQ Access initiative, Phasecraft announced on 6 November. Applications open in late November 2026 and the first cohort starts in spring 2027.
First software on SparQ

Simon Plant, deputy director at the NQCC, said the deal "marks the first time we are making quantum software available through our SparQ programme." The centre has until now focused on giving UK users access to quantum hardware.
Three tools

Participants will work with one of three Phasecraft tools. Magritte is for materials and molecular modelling, covering resource estimation and quantum circuit construction. Monet is a quantum-enhanced density functional theory tool for modelling materials and molecules. Mondrian is a quantum-enhanced optimisation platform for problems in areas such as finance, logistics or infrastructure, available through a web interface or API.
Who can apply

The NQCC and Phasecraft will invite proposals from UK businesses and researchers with challenges in materials science, chemistry and optimisation, with support from Phasecraft's scientists and engineers. Places are also reserved for the NQCC and academics doing non-commercial research.

body: Physical Superintelligence PBC posted on X on 6 November 2026: "Today Physical Superintelligence PBC is announcing a proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, one of the central open problems in quantum complexity, with major implications for quantum computing speedup." The verified @psipbc account is the company's primary public statement so far.

David Turturean, who the company later credits with leading the work, wrote on X: "A research system I built for @psipbc, using a non-public Anthropic model, has proved the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture! Open since 2008..." Photon Dispatch treats that wording as his account of the run, consistent with the company page.

Company research page (PSI's claim). On the same day PSI published A proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, dated 6 November 2026. According to that page, an internal research system running instances of a non-public Anthropic model on PSI infrastructure produced a complete proof on day three of a run; Lean accepted it; the system later improved the result twice, with Lean accepting the final version. PSI says the proof builds on ideas from Shachar Lovett and Jiapeng Zhang, David Reimer and others. Those steps, the Lean acceptance claim and the mathematical details are PSI's own account. Independent peer review of the full manuscript may still be pending.

What PSI says the result would mean. PSI frames the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture as addressing whether quantum computers can be exponentially faster than classical ones on random inputs that lack rare structure. The company says that, with the conjecture proved, an ordinary computer can predict a quantum computer's yes/no answer probability (up to small error, for all but a small fraction of strings) with a number of looks that grows at most like a fixed power of the quantum look count T—not exponentially. In PSI's words, on yes-or-no questions a quantum computer cannot save exponentially many looks unless the input has a rare pattern. That implication is stated by PSI; outsiders should wait for independent verification before treating it as settled mathematics.

Stanford group reading the proof. PSI says Guy Blanc, Jordan Docter, Carmen Strassle and Li-Yang Tan of Stanford, who in August 2026 settled a special case of the conjecture's prediction for algorithms with a fixed number of parallel rounds, have been reading the full proof, sent comments and are writing a shorter exposition. PSI quotes them as writing: "This is a huge result. It resolves a decades-old conjecture with important implications for the nature of problems that admit quantum speedups. The proof draws on and extends several lines of work in the analysis of boolean functions and probabilistic combinatorics. Everything is brought together in a rather magical way." The quote appears on PSI's page; Photon Dispatch has not independently confirmed the Stanford correspondence beyond that posting.

Contributors named by PSI. The page credits David Turturean with leading the work (research system, problem scoping, run, draft packaging and responsibility for correctness); Jim Halverson with auditing the proof; and Phiala Shanahan with comments on the Lean formalization.

What to watch. A publicly posted Lean formalization, an arXiv or journal manuscript, and independent expert write-ups (including any Stanford exposition) would let outsiders check the claim beyond the company announcement. Until then, the story rests on PSI's X post, Turturean's X post and PSI's research page.

title: Quantinuum maps Nexus developer platform path towards fault tolerant computing
summary: Quantinuum has outlined a multi generation Nexus roadmap designed to connect application development with successive quantum hardware systems, including Apollo, which it plans for 2029.
body: Quantinuum has unveiled a roadmap for its Nexus developer platform, setting out how the software is intended to evolve alongside the company’s quantum hardware towards a fault tolerant computing era.

The company announced the plan on 5 November. It describes Nexus as a platform that brings together programming, validation, compilation and execution, with a roadmap intended to automate more of the work involved in building and deploying quantum applications.

The plan is aligned with successive generations of Quantinuum hardware, including Apollo, which the company says is planned as its first universal, fully fault tolerant quantum computer in 2029. That timing is a company target, not a guarantee of delivery.

Quantinuum divides the platform’s intended development into three broad stages: develop, optimise and deploy. The develop stage is expected to include pre built primitives, fault tolerant libraries and domain specific tools, with increasing automation of error correction encoding, compilation and resource management.

The optimise stage is intended to provide tools for analysing runtime behaviour, resource requirements and application performance. Future releases are expected to add further error suppression, real time monitoring and more automated error recovery.

The deploy stage is designed to coordinate quantum and classical computing across Quantinuum processors, high performance computing systems, cloud infrastructure and third party tools. The aim is to let organisations integrate quantum workflows into existing computing environments.

The company says Nexus already supports more than 200 organisations, up 45 per cent in 2026. It also reports that job submissions increased tenfold in the 12 months through August 2026 compared with the preceding 12 month period.

Quantinuum says developers can already apply supported error correction techniques to programs and run supported programs on its Helios system. A further release planned for December is expected to expand hybrid workflows, add supported error correction codes and provide execution analytics.
The roadmap is a statement of intended product development. Its future capabilities, adoption and hardware milestones remain subject to delivery and should be read as company plans.

title: ORNL, IBM and AMD Launch Co-Design Platform for Quantum Error Correction
summary: IBM, Oak Ridge’s Quantum Science Center and AMD unveiled a co-design platform on 5 Nov 2026 pairing IBM’s 120-qubit Nighthawk with ORNL’s Umbra HPC system (AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs and 5th Gen EPYC CPUs) for quantum error-correction research aimed at DOE’s 2028 goals.
body: IBM, the Department of Energy-funded Quantum Science Center at Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) and AMD announced on 5 November 2026 a co-design platform for quantum error correction that integrates quantum processors with high-performance classical computing. Matching posts from ORNL and AMD describe the same launch.

What is being co-located. According to the partners, the first deployment puts IBM quantum computers—including the 120-qubit IBM Quantum Nighthawk—beside ORNL’s Umbra HPC system, powered by AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs and 5th Gen AMD EPYC CPUs. AMD’s compute is described as the classical foundation for error-correction research, decoder optimisation and software orchestration. The Quantum Insider flagged the launch on X with a link to its write-up.

DOE context the partners cite. The releases tie the work to DOE’s Quantum Genesis Mission and the Q Competition target of 100 logical qubits running 100,000 hard operations by late 2028. IBM says its current published progress on the Quantum Advantage Tracker includes experiments with up to 70 logical qubits and 438 hard operations, so closing the gap would require roughly a 230-fold increase in hard-operation count. Those figures are IBM’s stated tracker numbers, not an independent audit for this article.

What the platform is for. IBM says Nighthawk’s square-lattice connectivity, circuit throughput and real-time pulse control let researchers compare error-correction methods by qubits, time, samples and classical resources, and see where GPU nodes on Umbra help most. The partners say the platform will connect with the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility so quantum work can sit inside a broader AI and scientific computing stack. Planned research themes listed in the releases include concatenated and space-time codes, algorithm-aware decoders, hardware-aware circuit optimisation and compilation, and software orchestration.

Caveats. This is a research testbed announcement, not a claim that fault-tolerant quantum computing has been achieved. No new logical-error rates, decoder latencies or end-to-end QEC benchmarks from the co-located Nighthawk–Umbra stack were published in the launch notes reviewed here. Treat hardware specs, DOE targets and IBM’s tracker figures as attributed partner statements pending peer-reviewed results from the platform.
analysis: Hybrid QEC stacks that put classical GPUs next to superconducting processors are the path most large vendors describe for scaling beyond NISQ demos. ORNL’s Umbra + IBM Nighthawk pairing is notable because it is framed explicitly around DOE’s 2028 hard-operation goal rather than a consumer product launch—but the useful science still depends on decoder and code results that have not shipped with this announcement.

On 22 October 2026, Carolyn Mercer wrote on LinkedIn that she "Got to witness NASA’s first air-to-ground quantum entanglement demonstration this afternoon at the NASA Glenn Research Center. This technology is fundamental to future science missions that will explore the universe via entangled sensor networks." Mercer’s post credits Margaret Nazario’s team and Azlin Biaggi-Labiosa for funding vision. Note the wording difference: Glenn’s X post says photons were sent "over a quantum channel"; Mercer calls what she witnessed a "quantum entanglement demonstration." This desk is not treating those two phrases as interchangeable quotes.

A search for a matching November 2026 nasa.gov news release describing this specific air-to-ground quantum photon / entanglement flight did not turn up a public press page at the time of writing. Until NASA publishes a formal release with methods, dates, aircraft, link distance and measured metrics, the primary public claims remain Glenn’s X post and Mercer’s LinkedIn note. College Park, Maryland–based IonQ presented the agreement as compute procurement rather than a hardware installation in Connecticut. Access is through IonQ's cloud, so participating groups run jobs on IonQ's trapped-ion machines remotely. title: IonQ Completes $1.15 Billion All-Stock Acquisition of Elisity
summary: IonQ has closed its all-stock purchase of Zero Trust security company Elisity, issuing $1.15 billion in common stock, with up to $150 million more tied to revenue milestones.
body: IonQ has completed its acquisition of Elisity, a Zero Trust network security company, in an all-stock deal, the quantum computing company said on 4 November. IonQ announced the closing on X: "Today, IonQ completed its acquisition of @ElisityInc. Security has always been about protecting what matters most, and quantum makes that more urgent."

The terms. According to IonQ's press release, IonQ issued $1.15 billion of consideration in common stock at closing under the merger agreement. The sellers may earn up to a further $150 million based on Elisity's performance against revenue milestones through January 2028. That extra amount is contingent and was not paid at closing.

What Elisity does. Elisity helps organisations discover the devices connected to their networks, understand network risk and enforce identity-based Zero Trust policies, an approach that does not automatically trust anything just because it is inside the network. IonQ says it will combine this with its post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and quantum key distribution (QKD) products, so customers can use Elisity's view of their networks to decide where to deploy quantum-safe protection first.

The pitch targets "Harvest Now, Decrypt Later" attacks, where encrypted data is stolen today in the hope that a future quantum computer can break it. "Enterprise and government organizations will now be able to draw on one security architecture to contain attacks operating at machine speed today, and protect sensitive information against future quantum threats," IonQ chairman and CEO Niccolo de Masi said in the release.

Customers and leadership. The release says Elisity has more than 100 established enterprise deployments and will continue to serve customers under its current leadership, with existing deployments and identity policies carried forward. Elisity CEO James Winebrenner said the company would "extend the Elisity platform customers already use to help them prepare for post-quantum cryptography."

What to watch. The deal pushes IonQ further into security, alongside its computing and networking businesses. Whether the combined products win new customers, and whether Elisity hits the revenue milestones behind the $150 million earnout, will become clearer over the next two years.

title: Alice & Bob says 22,593 cat qubits could factor RSA-2048 in 3.14 days, in a new estimate
summary: Alice & Bob's new preprint estimates that a fault-tolerant machine built from its cat qubits could factor RSA-2048 with 22,593 physical qubits in 3.14 days. It is a resource estimate on paper, not a demonstration, and it assumes hardware no one has built yet.
body: Short answer: Alice & Bob, the Paris- and Boston-based company building superconducting "cat qubit" processors, estimates that a machine on its architecture could factor a 2048-bit RSA number with 22,593 physical qubits running for 3.14 days. The figure comes from a ten-author preprint posted to the IACR Cryptology ePrint Archive (2026/2665) on 28 October, which the company described in a blog post as "about 23 000 physical qubits and about three days to break RSA-2048." It is a resource estimate, not an attack run on real hardware.

A cat qubit stores information in a superconducting resonator holding many photons. Alice & Bob's design suppresses bit flips, where a qubit's 0 turns into 1 or the reverse, in the hardware itself, so the error-correcting code layered on top only has to catch phase flips. That is why the company can claim far fewer physical qubits per logical qubit than designs that must correct both kinds of error. For the difference between the two, see our explainer on what a logical qubit is.

According to Quantum Brief, the company credits three changes for the lower count: the cat qubits themselves, LDPC-cat codes published in 2024 that replace the repetition code used in its 2023 estimate, and a rebuilt adder that runs at a steady clock instead of pausing to wait on error-correction results. The switch to LDPC-cat codes alone took the RSA-2048 count from 49,649 to 22,593, according to Alice & Bob's release.

The headline number rests on four stated assumptions: an error-correction cycle of 1 microsecond, a 10-microsecond reaction time for the classical decoder, a phase-flip probability of 5×10<sup>-4</sup>, and no bit flips at all. Alice & Bob's notes to editors say zero bit flips is equivalent to a bit-flip time of about a century, and that if bit flips arrived about once an hour, RSA-2048 would need roughly 45,000 qubits.

The design can also trade size for speed. Spread across 610,530 cat qubits in ten machines, the RSA-2048 job would take about 1.25 hours, while 21,188 qubits would stretch it to 8.08 days, according to the paper's trade-off table as reported by Quantum Brief. The same paper puts the 256-bit elliptic-curve discrete logarithm, which underpins ECDSA signatures and ECDH key exchange, at no more than 29,588 physical qubits and 61.8 minutes.

For context, Craig Gidney and Martin Ekerå put RSA-2048 at about 20 million physical qubits in 2019, and Gidney, at Google Quantum AI, brought it below one million in 2025, figures Alice & Bob cites in its own post. The company says its new figure needs about 40 times fewer physical qubits than Gidney's 2025 estimate, under different hardware assumptions. In October Iceberg Quantum put the figure at about 48,000 physical qubits for its own architecture; see our report on Pinnacle 1.2. The Quantum Insider also covered the estimate.
analysis: The estimate is detailed engineering on paper, but the gap between paper and hardware is the whole story. The largest chip Alice & Bob described in its 20 October results from France's PROQCIMA programme had 12 qubits, and the company itself reported "a logical error rate not yet below threshold," as Quantum Brief notes. The no-bit-flip assumption is also well beyond what the company has measured on a single cat qubit. Estimates from different companies rest on different hardware assumptions, so a lower number is not directly comparable to a surface-code figure from Google.

What the trend does support is the advice that already exists. Each new estimate has cut the projected machine size, which strengthens the case for the timetable in NIST IR 8547: RSA and elliptic-curve public-key algorithms deprecated after 2030 and disallowed after 2035. Organisations planning that move can start with the standards that already exist; our explainer covers what ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA each do. Nothing in this paper means RSA-2048 can be broken today.
disclaimer: Figures are Alice & Bob's own resource estimates from a preprint that has not been peer reviewed, and they have not been independently verified. This is not a security assessment of any particular system.

title: What is FN-DSA? NIST's Falcon signature standard, and why FIPS 206 isn't published yet
summary: Checked on csrc.nist.gov on 2 November 2026, FIPS 206 for FN-DSA, NIST's planned Falcon-based signature standard, still has no public draft.
body: Short answer: FN-DSA is the name NIST plans to give FIPS 206, a digital-signature standard based on the Falcon scheme. Checked on csrc.nist.gov on 2 November 2026, FIPS 206 has not been published, not even as an initial public draft. NIST's post-quantum cryptography project page says the Falcon algorithm "was selected for ongoing standardization" and "that process is underway," and the agency's selected-algorithms list still marks Falcon "FIPS coming soon."

NIST picked Falcon in July 2022, alongside CRYSTALS-Dilithium and SPHINCS+, as one of the algorithms it would standardize after its multi-year public competition. Dilithium and SPHINCS+ became FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA) in August 2024; Falcon was held back for its own standard, which NIST calls FN-DSA. The other post-quantum standard still pending is HQC, a backup encryption algorithm NIST selected in March 2025; see PhotonDispatch's explainer on what HQC does. Our explainer on what ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA each do covers the three standards that did ship in 2024.

NIST has described the FIPS 206 draft as close to finished without publishing it. Writing on NIST's public pqc-forum mailing list on 28 August 2025, Dustin Moody, who leads the agency's post-quantum cryptography project, said the draft was "essentially completed on our end" and had gone up for internal approval to publish. He said the draft keeps Falcon's randomized signing rather than switching to a deterministic variant, and that NIST adjusted the Gaussian sampler used in key generation after consulting the Falcon submission team.

The delay traces to how Falcon signs. Falcon's reference design samples from a Gaussian distribution using floating-point arithmetic, which is hard to make both fast and resistant to timing side channels that could leak secret-key information. In correspondence posted to pqc-forum in September 2025, NIST said it would let implementers use fixed-point arithmetic for one step of key generation, but ruled out fixed-point signing because it would need roughly 256 bits per value. For signing itself, FIPS 206 will allow either native or software-emulated floating point, and NIST said it secured permission from IEEE to reprint the needed parts of the IEEE 754-2019 floating-point standard so FIPS 206 would not require a separate paid reference.

FN-DSA will sit alongside, not replace, the two 2024 signature standards, and all three rest on different math. ML-DSA is built on structured, or module, lattices and signs using the Fiat-Shamir-with-aborts technique from its CRYSTALS-Dilithium submission. SLH-DSA is a stateless hash-based scheme descended from SPHINCS+, which only relies on the security of its underlying hash function. FN-DSA is also lattice-based, but over NTRU lattices rather than module lattices, using the hash-and-sign framework of Gentry, Peikert and Vaikuntanathan with a technique Falcon's designers call fast Fourier sampling, according to the Falcon specification. NIST's 2030 and 2035 migration deadlines, covered in PhotonDispatch's report on IR 8547, apply to the older algorithms FN-DSA and its two finished siblings are meant to eventually replace; see our policy coverage for the wider transition.

Falcon's appeal is size. In the algorithm's pre-standardization specification, Falcon-512, roughly matched to NIST's security category 1, produces a 666-byte signature with an 897-byte public key; Falcon-1024, at category 5, produces a 1,280-byte signature with a 1,793-byte public key. For comparison, NIST's FIPS 204 specifies a 2,420-byte signature and a 1,312-byte public key for the smallest ML-DSA parameter set, ML-DSA-44, and FIPS 205 specifies a 7,856-byte signature but only a 32-byte public key for the smallest SLH-DSA parameter set. These Falcon figures are from the designers' own specification, published before NIST finished adapting the algorithm into FIPS 206, so the final numbers in the standard could still move slightly.

Smaller signatures matter most where many of them accumulate: a TLS handshake that chains several certificates, a DNSSEC response, a firmware update that gets re-verified at every boot, or a device with a narrow radio link. NIST has not given a publication date for FIPS 206. Outside trackers that monitor the agency's own pages put a final standard in late 2026 or early 2027, but that is their estimate, not a NIST commitment, so check csrc.nist.gov directly before planning around it.
analysis: FN-DSA looks like a near-complete standard, not an abandoned one: NIST says the specification text is largely finished and the holdup is about implementation safety, chiefly making floating-point signing resistant to timing side channels, not a weakness found in Falcon's underlying math. Organizations that need a post-quantum signature today should keep using ML-DSA or SLH-DSA, as NIST already recommends. FN-DSA is worth watching for size-constrained deployments once FIPS 206 is final, not a reason to delay adopting the standards that already exist.
disclaimer: This article describes standards NIST has published or is developing. It is not legal advice and not a configuration guide for any particular system. Figures for FN-DSA are from the pre-standardization Falcon specification and may change before FIPS 206 is finalized.

title: What is HQC? NIST's backup to ML-KEM, explained
summary: According to NIST, HQC is a code-based encryption algorithm chosen in March 2025 as a backup to ML-KEM, with a final standard expected in 2027.
body: Short answer: HQC is a post-quantum encryption algorithm that NIST selected on 11 March 2025 as a backup for ML-KEM, the main standard for general encryption. It is built on different mathematics, error-correcting codes rather than structured lattices, so that a weakness found in ML-KEM would not take both down at once.

Some background first. In August 2024 NIST finalized three post-quantum standards. FIPS 203 covers ML-KEM, a key-encapsulation mechanism: a way for two parties to agree a shared secret key over a public network. FIPS 204 and FIPS 205 cover digital signatures. Our explainer on what ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA each do goes through them one by one.

HQC fills a narrow role. NIST says it is not intended to replace ML-KEM, which remains the recommended choice for general encryption. Dustin Moody, who heads NIST's Post-Quantum Cryptography project, said organizations should keep migrating to the standards finalized in 2024, and that NIST wanted "a backup standard that is based on a different math approach than ML-KEM."

The difference in mathematics is the whole point. ML-KEM is built around structured lattices. HQC is built around error-correcting codes, an idea NIST notes has been used in information security for decades. If a new attack, quantum or classical, turned out to weaken lattice schemes, a code-based scheme would not automatically fall with it.

There is a cost. Moody said HQC is a lengthier algorithm than ML-KEM and demands more computing resources, but its clean and secure operation convinced reviewers it would be a worthy backup. HQC was the only algorithm standardized from NIST's fourth round of candidates, which began with four algorithms meriting further study.

On timing, NIST said in March 2025 that it planned to issue a draft standard incorporating HQC in about a year, with a finalized standard expected in 2027. Check NIST's Computer Security Resource Center for the current status of that draft before relying on a date. For the wider migration deadlines, see our piece on NIST IR 8547 and the 2030 and 2035 dates.
analysis: For most organizations HQC changes nothing today: NIST's own advice is to keep moving to ML-KEM and the 2024 signature standards. Its value is insurance. Having a second key-establishment standard built on unrelated mathematics gives a fallback if lattice cryptanalysis improves, which is the same logic NIST applied when it described SLH-DSA as a backup signature method. Selecting HQC is not a sign that ML-KEM has been broken.
disclaimer: This article describes NIST announcements. It is not legal advice and not a configuration guide for any particular system.

title: Harvest now, decrypt later: why encrypted data is already at risk from quantum computers
summary: Harvest now, decrypt later means recording encrypted traffic today and breaking it once a large quantum computer exists. Here is how the threat works and why it sets the migration clock.
body: Short answer: "Harvest now, decrypt later" describes an attacker who copies encrypted data today, stores it, and waits until a large enough quantum computer can break the public key cryptography that protected it. The data does not need to be decrypted now to be at risk now. That is why governments ask organisations to move to post-quantum cryptography years before such a machine exists.

Most internet encryption uses two layers. A public key method such as RSA or elliptic curve Diffie Hellman agrees a shared secret, and a symmetric cipher such as AES then encrypts the actual data with that secret. A sufficiently large quantum computer running Shor's algorithm could recover the secret from the recorded key exchange, and with it the data. Symmetric ciphers are much less exposed; the main defence there is using adequately long keys.

The risk depends on how long the data must stay secret. If information will still matter in ten or fifteen years, such as health records, state secrets, long term contracts or intellectual property, then traffic captured today could become readable within its useful life. Short lived data, such as a one time login code, matters far less.

The answer is to change the key exchange, not to wait. NIST published FIPS 203 in August 2024, which standardises ML-KEM, a key encapsulation mechanism designed to resist quantum attack. Our guide to ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA explains what each standard does. Many deployments use a hybrid approach that combines a classical exchange with ML-KEM, so the connection stays secure if either one holds.

Official timelines reflect this. NIST's draft report IR 8547 proposes deprecating quantum vulnerable public key algorithms at the 112 bit security level after 2030 and disallowing them after 2035; we covered it in our report on the draft. The UK's NCSC sets milestones of 2028 for discovery and planning, 2031 for priority migrations and 2035 for completing migration.
analysis: Opinion: Nobody can say when a cryptographically relevant quantum computer will arrive, and estimates have moved repeatedly. Harvest now, decrypt later turns that uncertainty into a simple planning question: how long must this data stay private, and how long will migration take? If the sum reaches past the earliest plausible date, the work should already be under way.
disclaimer: This is a general explainer, not security advice for any specific system. Dates are from the NIST and NCSC documents linked below.

title: Quantum error correction basics: syndromes, thresholds and why overhead matters
summary: Quantum error correction detects errors through parity-check measurements and, below a hardware threshold, makes encoded qubits more reliable as codes grow, according to the research literature.
body: Short answer: Quantum error correction protects quantum information by encoding it redundantly across many qubits, repeatedly measuring parity checks that reveal errors without revealing the data, and using a classical decoder to work out and undo the most likely errors. It only helps if the hardware's error rate is below a threshold, and it costs many physical qubits per protected qubit.

Quantum computers suffer two basic kinds of error: bit flips, which swap 0 and 1, and phase flips, which change the sign relationship in a superposition. Real noise is continuous, but measuring a code's parity checks forces it into one of a discrete set of outcomes, so correcting bit flips and phase flips is enough to handle general errors. Gottesman's introduction to the field sets out this 'discretisation of errors' and the stabilizer formalism most codes are built on.

The pattern of parity-check results is called the syndrome. In each round of error correction, helper qubits interact with groups of data qubits and are measured; a change in the syndrome flags an error nearby. A decoder, which is ordinary classical software or hardware, takes the stream of syndromes and decides which correction to apply. It has to keep pace with the machine. Google Quantum AI's 2024 Nature paper reported an average decoder latency of 63 microseconds at distance 5 with a 1.1-microsecond cycle time, running for up to a million cycles.

The threshold theorem is what makes the approach worthwhile. In the 1990s Dorit Aharonov and Michael Ben-Or, among others, showed that if each component's error probability is below some constant threshold, arbitrarily long quantum computations can be made reliable with only polylogarithmic overhead, by using codes within codes. Modern surface-code estimates put the threshold for realistic noise near 1% per operation, according to Fowler and colleagues' 2012 review.

Overhead is the catch. Fowler's review estimated that useful fault-tolerant machines would need very large numbers of physical qubits, because each logical qubit uses hundreds to thousands of them and some operations need extra resources, such as 'magic states', to complete a universal gate set. Lower physical error rates, better decoders and more efficient codes all shrink that overhead, which is why researchers track the logical error rate per cycle and how fast it falls as codes grow.

Experiments have begun to show the expected behaviour. Google reported in 2024 that its distance-7 surface-code memory on the Willow chip had an error rate of 0.143% per cycle, and that each increase of two in code distance cut the logical error rate by a factor of 2.14. The same paper noted that rare correlated error events, roughly once an hour, limited its longest repetition-code runs.
analysis: Error correction has moved from theory to engineering, but the open questions are practical: how to handle correlated errors, how to decode fast enough at scale, and how many physical qubits a useful machine will really need. Resource estimates differ widely depending on hardware assumptions, so a single number for 'qubits needed' should be read with its assumptions attached.

title: What is a logical qubit, and why do quantum computers need them?
summary: A logical qubit is one unit of quantum information spread across many physical qubits so that errors can be detected and corrected, as described in surface-code research.
body: Short answer: A logical qubit is a qubit built out of many physical qubits. The quantum information is spread across the group in a pattern, called an error-correcting code, so that errors on individual physical qubits can be detected and fixed without reading out, and destroying, the information itself.

Physical qubits, whether superconducting circuits, trapped ions or neutral atoms, are fragile. Heat, stray fields and imperfect control pulses flip or blur their states, and today's best hardware still makes errors far more often than long, useful algorithms are expected to tolerate. A logical qubit is the field's answer: rather than waiting for perfect hardware, it adds redundancy.

The idea can't simply copy classical backup. The no-cloning theorem says an unknown quantum state cannot be copied, and measuring a qubit directly collapses it. Error-correcting codes get around this by measuring only joint properties of groups of qubits, called stabilizers or parity checks. Those checks reveal whether, and roughly where, an error happened, but say nothing about the encoded value, as Daniel Gottesman's widely used introduction to the subject explains.

The most studied design is the surface code, in which physical qubits sit on a two-dimensional grid and neighbouring groups are checked over and over in rounds. Austin Fowler and colleagues' 2012 review describes how logical qubits are formed on such a grid and how operations between them are carried out. The size of a surface-code logical qubit is set by its code distance, d: a distance-d code needs on the order of 2d² physical qubits including the measurement helpers, and can correct any combination of fewer than about d/2 errors.

Bigger is only better if the hardware is good enough. Below a hardware error rate called the threshold, each step up in code distance makes the logical qubit more reliable; above it, adding qubits makes things worse. In a paper published in Nature in December 2024, Google Quantum AI reported a 101-qubit distance-7 surface-code memory on its Willow processor with an error rate of 0.143% per error-correction cycle, and said the logical error rate fell by a factor of 2.14 each time the distance grew by two. The team also reported that the logical memory outlived its best physical qubit by a factor of 2.4.

Other hardware approaches use the same concept. A Harvard-led team reported in Nature in 2023 a neutral-atom processor that ran circuits with up to 48 logical qubits using a small error-detecting code, and improved a logical two-qubit gate by moving from a distance-3 to a distance-7 surface code.
analysis: Logical qubit counts are now a common headline number, but they aren't directly comparable between announcements. Codes differ in how many errors they can correct, some experiments detect errors without correcting them, and a logical qubit used only as a memory is not the same as one that can run a full set of gates. When reading a claim, look for the code distance, the logical error rate per cycle or per operation, and whether the result has been peer reviewed.

title: NIST says quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms are deprecated after 2030 and disallowed after 2035
summary: According to NIST IR 8547, published 27 October 2026, quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms are deprecated after 2030 and disallowed after 2035.
body: Short answer: On 27 October 2026 the US National Institute of Standards and Technology published NIST IR 8547, Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards. NIST says it will deprecate quantum-vulnerable public-key cryptography after 2030 and disallow its use under NIST standards and guidelines after 2035.

The report is dated October 2026. Its publication history says the NIST Editorial Review Board approved it on 21 October 2026, and both NIST's news post and the Computer Security Resource Center list 27 October 2026. It is the agency's plan for moving off public-key methods that a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer could break, toward the post-quantum standards NIST finished in 2024: FIPS 203 (ML-KEM) for key establishment, and FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA) for signatures. Dustin Moody, the NIST mathematician who leads the project, said there is "not one strategy that fits all use cases".

For signatures, NIST's table covers ECDSA, EdDSA and RSA as specified in FIPS 186, at the parameter sets it still treats as approved: at least 112 bits of classical security for ECDSA and RSA, and at least 128 bits for EdDSA. Each is marked deprecated after 2030 and disallowed after 2035. The same window applies to quantum-vulnerable key establishment in Special Publications 800-56A and 800-56B: finite-field and elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman and MQV, and RSA key establishment, again from 112 bits of classical security upward. NIST says this replaces an older plan, in SP 800-57 Part 1, to disallow public-key schemes offering 112 bits of security on 1 January 2031.

National Security Memorandum 10 still names 2035 as the target for finishing the migration across federal systems, the report says. Executive Order 14412 and OMB Memorandum M-26-15, as the report describes them, pull the most sensitive systems forward: high-value assets and high-impact systems are to adopt post-quantum key establishment by 31 December 2030 and post-quantum digital signatures by 31 December 2031. NIST says the broader 2030-2035 window does not relax those earlier deadlines. The report also says Executive Order 14306 and the same OMB memo require agencies to support TLS 1.3 no later than 2 January 2030.

NIST says ML-KEM, specified in FIPS 203, is at present the only approved post-quantum key-establishment scheme based on public-key cryptography, and it recommends the ML-KEM-768 parameter set as the default. HQC has been chosen for a future standard; NIST says it becomes an approved scheme after that standard is published. Symmetric cryptography is on a different footing: the report says approved symmetric primitives with at least 128 bits of classical security are believed to meet at least Category 1 on NIST's post-quantum scale, while a few symmetric standards at the 112-bit level are to be disallowed in 2030.
analysis: In the report's own glossary, a deprecated algorithm may still be used if the data owner accepts the risk, while a disallowed algorithm is no longer allowed for the stated purpose. The December 2030 and December 2031 dates apply to the sensitive federal systems the report names. They are not, on the text of IR 8547, an automatic cutoff for every deployment of RSA.
disclaimer: Dates and requirements are NIST's, as stated in IR 8547 and the agency's 27 October 2026 news post. This is not legal advice, and it is not a finding about any particular system.

title: IQM says Emerald entangled all 54 qubits, with a GHZ fidelity of 0.516
summary: IQM says its Emerald cloud system prepared a 54-qubit GHZ state at fidelity 0.516 with readout-error mitigation, just above 0.5.
body: Short answer: IQM Quantum Computers said on 29 October 2026 that its cloud-accessible Emerald processor had entangled all 54 qubits on the chip at the same time. IQM measured a Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger fidelity of 0.516 for the full chip when readout-error mitigation was applied, and 0.515 for a 40-qubit version of the same test without that mitigation. The company says both numbers sit above 0.500, the line it uses to separate genuine multipartite entanglement from noise.

The state was prepared across the whole Emerald chip, IQM says, by an automated routine that picks two-qubit gates and the order they run in, weighing gate quality against how long other qubits sit idle. Craig Ciesla, IQM's chief technology officer, said the result "came down to being smarter about how we prepare the state".

IQM says the demonstration follows about a year of hardware and calibration work: a revised calibration method, an updated gate set, and continued use of dynamical decoupling and qubit selection. The company says those changes cut the error rate of quantum operations in the processor by up to 50 percent. It also says that, before this run, a comparable demonstration on Emerald could reliably use on the order of 30 qubits inside a single algorithm, and that cloud customers can now call on that same full-chip performance.

The announcement was issued through Business Wire at 3:00 a.m. US Eastern time and datelined Espoo, Finland. IQM describes itself as a superconducting quantum-computing company founded in 2018 and listed on Nasdaq under the symbol IQMX.
IQM says the preparation routine is part of a wider effort to automate how its machines are operated and tuned, including calibration work the company describes as AI-driven.
analysis: The 54-qubit fidelity includes readout-error mitigation and the 40-qubit figure does not, so the two results are not a like-for-like picture of scaling. A fidelity of 0.516 is only slightly above the 0.5 line IQM cites. The figures are the company's, given in a press release rather than in a paper linked from that release.
disclaimer: Fidelity figures, the error-rate claim and the comparison with earlier Emerald runs are IQM's own statements and have not been independently verified. IQM Quantum Computers is listed on Nasdaq (IQMX). This is not investment advice.

title: What ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA each do in NIST's post-quantum standards
summary: According to NIST, FIPS 203, 204 and 205, effective 14 August 2024, cover key establishment (ML-KEM) and two signature methods (ML-DSA and SLH-DSA).
body: Short answer: The three post-quantum standards NIST finalized in August 2024 do different jobs. FIPS 203, ML-KEM, is for agreeing a shared secret key. FIPS 204, ML-DSA, is the primary standard for digital signatures. FIPS 205, SLH-DSA, is a second signature method, built on different mathematics, which NIST describes as a backup.

A key-encapsulation mechanism lets two parties derive a shared secret over a public network. NIST says ML-KEM, taken from the CRYSTALS-Kyber submission, is the main standard for general encryption, citing comparatively small keys and speed. ML-DSA, from CRYSTALS-Dilithium, is for signatures that tie a message to a signer and show whether it was changed. SLH-DSA, from SPHINCS+, is also a signature scheme. NIST says it uses a different mathematical approach from ML-DSA and is there as a backup should a weakness in ML-DSA turn up.

The Secretary of Commerce approved FIPS 203, 204 and 205, and the Federal Register notice (89 FR 66052) makes them effective on 14 August 2024. NIST's news post of 13 August 2024 said the documents include the algorithms, instructions for implementing them and the uses they are meant for, and that they were ready to use. Dustin Moody, who leads the project, said "full integration will take time."

In 2022 NIST selected four algorithms to standardize: CRYSTALS-Kyber, CRYSTALS-Dilithium, SPHINCS+ and FALCON. The August 2024 post said a draft based on FALCON, to be named FN-DSA, was still planned. NIST IR 8547, published in October 2026, says the agency is still developing a FIPS for a signature algorithm derived from FALCON, as a further alternative, and it recommends ML-KEM-768 as the default parameter set for FIPS 203. The 2030 and 2035 transition dates are set out in PhotonDispatch's report on that roadmap.

NIST says the new algorithms rest on math problems intended to resist both conventional computers and quantum computers, unlike factoring and discrete logarithms, which underlie widely used schemes such as RSA and elliptic-curve signatures. The agency describes the three 2024 standards as the primary tools for general encryption and for signatures, and says further algorithms are backups rather than a reason to wait.
analysis: Publishing a standard is not the same thing as finishing a migration, and it is not evidence that a quantum computer can break public-key encryption today. NIST's August 2024 announcement described a machine with that capability as a future possibility. Describing SLH-DSA as a backup was a design choice NIST stated at the time, not a report that ML-DSA had failed.
disclaimer: This article describes standards NIST has published. It is not legal advice and not a configuration guide for any particular system.

title: Quantinuum says Helios hit 99.9995% logical fidelity, a tenfold error-correction record
summary: Quantinuum says its Helios trapped-ion computer reached 99.9995% logical fidelity with a color code, about five errors per million operations.
body: Short answer: Quantinuum announced on 19 October 2026 that its Helios commercial quantum computer achieved a logical fidelity of 99.9995%, which the company says equals about five errors in a million operations. Quantinuum calls it a world record for quantum error correction.

According to the company, the error rate is 10 times lower than the record Quantinuum itself set in September 2026 and 100 times lower than the best published result on any other hardware type, which it says was reported by Google Quantum AI on a superconducting system.

The result used a well-known error-correcting scheme called a color code. Quantinuum says logical errors fell exponentially as it increased the code distance, with each tested step cutting the remaining errors by what it calls a record factor of 12.

The trade-off is qubit overhead. On Helios, Quantinuum says its earlier Helix code used 10 physical qubits per logical qubit, while the color code used up to 37, in exchange for lower logical error rates. Both studies ran on the same hardware.
Quantinuum says the accuracy is now within the target range for Apollo, its planned universal fault-tolerant quantum computer, which it expects to be available by 2029.
analysis: Comparisons of logical fidelity across companies depend on the codes, operations and benchmarks used. The figures here are Quantinuum's own and have not been independently replicated.
disclaimer: Figures and timelines are Quantinuum's own claims as stated in its press release and have not been independently verified. Quantinuum is a listed company (NASDAQ: QNT); this is not investment advice.

title: Google shows magic state cultivation on Willow, cutting errors about 40x
summary: Google Quantum AI says magic state cultivation worked on its Willow chip, cutting errors about 40-fold and yielding T-states at 99.99% logical fidelity.
body: Short answer: Google Quantum AI said on 15 October 2026 that it has demonstrated "magic state cultivation" on its Willow processor, reducing errors about 40 times compared with uncultivated states and producing T-states with a logical fidelity of 99.99%, which it calls a record. The work was published in Science the same day, according to Google.

Magic states are special quantum states needed to run the full set of operations that make a quantum computer universal. Google says producing high-quality, error-corrected magic states is so costly that some estimates put up to 95% of a machine's capacity into making them, and each one can only be used once.

Cultivation, developed in a 2024 theory paper by Google researchers Craig Gidney, Noah Shutty and Cody Jones, works like a filter: a noisy state is injected into a small patch of the chip and checked with coordinated measurements, and flawed attempts are thrown away, according to Google's description.

Google says the team also had to invent a new benchmarking method after lab noise from equipment drift and temperature changes undermined its usual measurement technique. It also moved purified states from a distance-3 color code into a distance-5 surface code, showing the states can survive the transfer on its hardware.
Google says cultivation still has to be shown at a larger scale and that plenty of technical challenges remain before it is practical.
